Actions & forms::Actions and forms.summary: React form Actions handle asynchronous mutations through function-valued action props. useActionState tracks returned state and pending work, while useFormStatus exposes a parent form’s status; Server Functions can provide progressive enhancement.
Actions & forms::Actions and forms.explanation: A form action can be wrapped with useActionState so each submission receives the previous state and FormData, returns updated state, and exposes whether the action is pending. A Server Function can enable progressive enhancement; useFormStatus lets a descendant read the parent form’s submission status.
Actions & forms::Actions and forms.syntax: const [state, action, isPending] = useActionState(reducerAction, initialState, permalink?);

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: The action or Server Function; with useActionState it receives the previous state and submitted FormData.

parameters.name: initialState
parameters.description: The initial value used for the action state before the first submission.

parameters.name: permalink
parameters.description: Optional stable URL used for progressive enhancement when submission occurs before JavaScript loads.

Actions & forms::Actions and forms.returns: useActionState returns the current state, a wrapped action, and a pending flag. useFormStatus returns form status information, including pending.

example.title: Action-backed form
example.explanation: The returned action is attached to the form, while the state and pending flag drive the result and submit UI.

useCases.title: Show action results
useCases.scenario: A mutation returns validation errors or updated data that the component must render.

useCases.title: Build pending feedback
useCases.scenario: A submit button should disable itself or show progress while the parent form is running.

useCases.title: Progressively enhance submissions
useCases.scenario: A form must remain submittable before the client bundle or hydration is ready.

useCases.title: Use formAction overrides
useCases.scenario: Different controls in one form need distinct function-based submit behavior.

interview.question: What does useActionState provide for a form mutation?
interview.answer: useActionState wraps an action and returns state plus a dispatch function, and React also provides a pending indicator for the action. The action receives the previous state and submitted FormData.
interview.followUp: How can the form work before hydration? Pass a Server Function through the form action, optionally supplying a permalink to useActionState so pre-JavaScript submission can navigate correctly.

interview.question: How does useFormStatus help build form feedback?
interview.answer: useFormStatus reads status information from the parent form. A descendant can use its pending value to disable a submit control or display progress.
interview.followUp: Why must the status-reading component be nested? The Hook reads the nearest parent form’s status rather than the status of an arbitrary form elsewhere in the tree.

interview.question: What does progressive enhancement mean for React form Actions?
interview.answer: React supports functions as form action handlers, and Server Functions can progressively enhance submissions. With the right setup, the browser can submit before the JavaScript bundle has loaded.
interview.followUp: How can an error appear before hydration? Render the form as a Client Component, use a Server Function as its action, and display the result returned through useActionState.

keyPoints: A successful function-based form action resets the form automatically after submission.
The hook stores the most recent action result so the component can render server or validation feedback.
A nested submit component can read its parent form’s status without receiving status props explicitly.
With Server Functions, React can replay submissions made before hydration completes.
gotchas: Call useActionState only from client code; it is a Hook and cannot be used directly in a Server Component.
Progressive enhancement requires the appropriate Server Function and form setup; client JavaScript is not required for the initial submission.

Actions & forms::Controlled inputs.summary: A controlled input gets its displayed value from React state rather than letting the DOM own it. Pass value or checked together with an onChange handler that synchronously updates the backing state.
Actions & forms::Controlled inputs.explanation: A controlled input receives its current text or selection state through React and reports user edits through onChange. Updating the backing state synchronously keeps React's value and the DOM aligned, making state the single source of truth for validation and coordinated updates.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: String containing the text for a controlled text input, or form data for a radio button.

parameters.name: checked
parameters.description: Boolean controlling whether a checkbox or radio button is selected.

parameters.name: onChange
parameters.description: Event handler that synchronously updates the controlled value.

example.title: A controlled text input
example.explanation: The state variable supplies the input's value, while onChange synchronously copies each DOM change into state.

useCases.title: Live validation
useCases.scenario: A field must show validation feedback immediately as the user types.

useCases.title: Coordinated updates
useCases.scenario: Several controls must update from one authoritative value.

useCases.title: State-driven form behavior
useCases.scenario: The submitted or displayed form data must be derived from current React state.

interview.question: How does a controlled input work?
interview.answer: A controlled input gets its current text from value, or its selection from checked for a checkbox or radio button. Its onChange handler must synchronously update the state that supplies that prop.
interview.followUp: What happens if the state is not updated during onChange? React re-renders the supplied value, so the DOM can revert after each keystroke.

interview.question: Which props make an input controlled?
interview.answer: Use value for a text input and checked for a checkbox or radio button. Pass an onChange handler that reads the new value and updates the backing state.
interview.followUp: Why use this pattern? It lets React state remain the authoritative value for validation and coordinated UI updates.

interview.question: When does onChange run and what is required of it?
interview.answer: onChange fires immediately when the user changes the input, including on every keystroke for text input. In React it behaves like the browser input event and is required for controlled inputs.
interview.followUp: What must the handler do? It must synchronously copy the new DOM value into the state represented by value or checked.

keyPoints: Pass value to control text input content, or checked to control checkbox and radio selection.
The value prop determines the text displayed by a controlled text input.
The checked prop determines whether a checkbox or radio button is selected.
Controlled input changes are observed immediately through onChange, including each text keystroke.
React treats the supplied controlled prop as authoritative and keeps the DOM aligned with it.
gotchas: If the handler does not synchronously update the state used by value or checked, React restores the previous supplied value after typing.
Supplying value or checked without the corresponding updater makes the input controlled but non-editable.

Actions & forms::Form status.summary: Use useFormStatus inside a form to read its submission state from a nested component. This enables pending UI without passing form status through intermediate components.
Actions & forms::Form status.explanation: useFormStatus reads submission information from the nearest parent form, allowing a nested component to react to pending, submitted data, method, or action without receiving status props. The component using the Hook must be rendered inside the form; it observes the parent form rather than forms created by itself or its children.
Actions & forms::Form status.syntax: const { pending, data, method, action } = useFormStatus();
Actions & forms::Form status.returns: A status object containing pending, data, method, and action. pending is boolean; data is FormData or null; method is 'get' or 'post'; action is the parent form's function reference or null.

example.title: Disable a submit button while the form is pending
example.explanation: The button reads the parent form's submission state directly and disables itself while the action is running.

useCases.title: Pending submit control
useCases.scenario: Disable a submit button and change its label while an action is running.

useCases.title: Submission-aware feedback
useCases.scenario: Display or inspect the FormData currently being submitted.

useCases.title: Reusable form components
useCases.scenario: Build reusable design-system controls that respond to their containing form.

interview.question: What does useFormStatus provide, and how is pending commonly used?
interview.answer: useFormStatus returns a status object for the parent form. Its pending property is true while that form is actively submitting, so a nested submit control can disable itself or show alternate text.
interview.followUp: What happens if the Hook is called outside a form? It cannot observe a submission context, so pending remains false.

interview.question: Where must a component using useFormStatus be rendered?
interview.answer: The component calling useFormStatus must be rendered inside the form whose status it needs. This lets reusable controls access the parent form state without receiving status through props.
interview.followUp: Does it observe a form rendered by the component itself? No; it only reports the status of a parent form.

interview.question: Which status fields besides pending can useFormStatus expose?
interview.answer: The returned data property contains the FormData currently being submitted, or null when there is no active submission or no parent form. method reports GET or POST, and action reports the parent form's function action when applicable.
interview.followUp: When is action null? It is null without a parent form, and also when the form action is a URI or is unspecified.

keyPoints: Read pending to switch a nested control between its idle and submitting UI.
Use data to inspect the values being submitted by the parent form.
The method field identifies whether the parent form submits with GET or POST.
gotchas: Calling the Hook outside a form does not provide that form's status.
A form rendered by the same component or by one of its children is not the form being observed.

Actions & forms::useActionState.summary: Pair an Action with its latest result and pending flag. useActionState is useful for async forms because the reducer receives the previous result and the submitted payload, enabling validation feedback and loading UI.
Actions & forms::useActionState.explanation: useActionState wraps an Action and tracks its latest result. At component scope, provide a reducer action and initial state; React returns that state, a dispatch function suitable for an Action or form action, and a pending flag. The reducer receives the previous state followed by the dispatched payload, so a form can render validation results while disabling controls during submission.
Actions & forms::useActionState.syntax: const [state, dispatchAction, isPending] = useActionState(reducerAction, initialState, permalink?)

parameters.name: reducerAction
parameters.description: Function invoked by the Action. It receives the previous state first, followed by the payload passed to the returned dispatch function.

parameters.name: initialState
parameters.description: Initial value for the tracked state. It is not used after the returned dispatch function is invoked for the first time.

parameters.name: permalink
parameters.description: Optional unique URL for the page modified by the form; useful when the form submission needs progressive enhancement across navigation.

Actions & forms::useActionState.returns: An array containing the current state, a dispatchAction function for Actions, and an isPending boolean indicating whether dispatched Actions for this Hook are pending.

example.title: Form validation with result and pending state
example.explanation: The returned form action receives FormData, while the reducer action also receives the previous result first. Each submission stores the reducer's returned value in state, and isPending indicates whether an Action dispatched through this hook is still running.

useCases.title: Render the latest submission result
useCases.scenario: A form needs to display server or validation feedback after each submission.

useCases.title: Disable controls while an Action is pending
useCases.scenario: A submit control should reflect asynchronous work.

useCases.title: Support progressive enhancement with a permalink
useCases.scenario: A form should work across navigation before client JavaScript finishes loading.

interview.question: What does useActionState return?
interview.answer: It returns exactly three values: the latest state, a dispatch function, and an isPending flag. The initial render uses initialState; later state is the reducer action's returned value.
interview.followUp: Why does the reducer receive two arguments? The first is the prior state, and the second is the payload passed when the returned dispatch function runs.

interview.question: How does the reducer action receive input and prior results?
interview.answer: The reducer action receives the previous state first and the dispatched payload second. With a form action, that payload is typically FormData, allowing the reducer to return validation or submission results.
interview.followUp: How can the result reach a form UI? Pass the returned dispatch function to the form's action prop and render the returned state.

interview.question: What rules apply to calling useActionState and its dispatch function?
interview.answer: Call the Hook at the top level of a component or custom Hook, not inside a condition or loop. Invoke its returned dispatch function from an Action, such as startTransition or a form action.
interview.followUp: What should be done when conditional logic seems necessary? Extract a component so the Hook remains unconditional at that component's top level.

keyPoints: It connects an Action to state, making the Action's latest result available to rendering code.
Initialize it during component rendering at the top level, rather than in event-driven or conditional code.
The reducer gets its prior result first, then the payload supplied to the returned dispatch function.
Its first returned value is the latest reducer result, beginning with the supplied initial state.
The second returned value is the wrapped function that triggers the reducer when used from an Action.
The third value supports loading UI, such as disabling a submit button while work is pending.
gotchas: Call useActionState only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; do not place it in loops or conditions.
The returned dispatch function must run inside an Action, such as a function passed to a form action or wrapped in startTransition.
The initialState argument is used only before the first dispatch; later renders use the reducer's previous returned value.

Async UI::Error boundaries.summary: Error boundaries isolate rendering failures and show fallback UI for the affected subtree. Use getDerivedStateFromError for fallback state and componentDidCatch for reporting.
Async UI::Error boundaries.explanation: An error boundary is a class component that surrounds part of the tree and substitutes fallback UI when a descendant fails while rendering. Implement getDerivedStateFromError to switch to fallback state, and optionally componentDidCatch for reporting; provide a recovery path such as retrying by remounting the failed subtree.

example.title: A rendering error boundary
example.explanation: Wrap the UI that should recover from rendering failures with the boundary. Replace Profile with a component whose render can fail to see the fallback.

useCases.title: Isolate a risky widget
useCases.scenario: A dashboard widget can fail independently of the rest of the page.

useCases.title: Keep surrounding navigation usable
useCases.scenario: A profile or settings panel may fail because of malformed data or a rendering bug.

useCases.title: Report while showing a safe fallback
useCases.scenario: A production failure should be visible to the team without exposing internal details to users.

useCases.title: Handle action failures
useCases.scenario: A React 19 form action throws during submission.

interview.question: How do you implement an Error Boundary?
interview.answer: An Error Boundary is a component that displays fallback UI instead of the subtree that crashed. A class component becomes one by defining static getDerivedStateFromError; componentDidCatch can additionally report the failure.
interview.followUp: What failures are outside its scope? It does not catch event-handler errors, server-side-rendering errors, errors from itself, or ordinary errors caught by code outside the child-rendering path.

interview.question: What are the roles of getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch?
interview.answer: Use getDerivedStateFromError to update state during the error path, then render fallback UI when that state is set. Use componentDidCatch for side effects such as sending an error to an error-reporting service.
interview.followUp: Why separate the two methods? State derivation determines what React renders, while componentDidCatch is the place for logging or other extra logic.

interview.question: Where should an Error Boundary be placed?
interview.answer: Place the boundary around the smallest UI region that can fail while still providing a useful fallback. React sends the failure to the nearest boundary, so nested boundaries can isolate independent parts of the interface.
interview.followUp: How does this relate to React 19 Actions? Errors thrown by a form action can be shown by wrapping the form in an Error Boundary; useActionState is another way to render an action error message.

keyPoints: A class component is an Error Boundary when it defines the rendering-error lifecycle methods.
The boundary replaces the failed descendant area with fallback content rather than leaving the user with a blank result.
componentDidCatch is suitable for reporting failures to monitoring or analytics systems.
React invokes the static method for rendering failures from descendants, including deeply nested children.
componentDidCatch receives descendant rendering failures after they reach the boundary.
gotchas: They do not handle event-handler failures, server-rendering failures, or errors thrown by the boundary itself.
A surrounding JavaScript try/catch is not a substitute for an Error Boundary when a child fails during rendering.
Without a boundary, a rendering failure can remove the application UI instead of showing a fallback.

Async UI::Suspense and use.summary: Read a Promise or context during rendering with use. A Suspense boundary supplies fallback UI while a Promise is pending, and an Error Boundary handles rejection.
Async UI::Suspense and use.explanation: Pass a cached Promise to a component and call use during rendering. While the Promise is pending, the nearest Suspense boundary renders its fallback; after resolution, React retries the component and renders the returned value. Rejected Promises are handled by the nearest Error Boundary.

parameters.name: resource
parameters.description: A Promise or context resource whose value should be read during rendering.

Async UI::Suspense and use.returns: The resolved Promise value or the current context value.

example.title: Read a Promise inside Suspense
example.explanation: Pass a cached Promise into the component, read it with use, and let the nearest Suspense boundary show fallback UI until the Promise resolves.

useCases.title: Async data display
useCases.scenario: Render data loaded by a Suspense-enabled framework without local loading state.

useCases.title: Progressive UI loading
useCases.scenario: Show a skeleton while a lazily loaded component or streamed Server Component becomes ready.

useCases.title: Conditional context access
useCases.scenario: Read context only in a particular branch or iteration where it is needed.

keyPoints: use reads a Promise or context during rendering.
A component pauses rendering while its Promise is pending.
Suspense provides the temporary UI shown during the wait.
Promise rejection is routed to the nearest Error Boundary.
A boundary reveals its children only when the suspended content is ready.
gotchas: Do not catch use directly with try-catch; place the component under an Error Boundary instead.
Call use only while rendering a component or custom Hook.
Do not inspect Promise internals to bypass React; pass the Promise to use.

Foundations::Components & JSX.summary: React components are JavaScript functions that return JSX, a stricter HTML-like syntax for describing UI. Pass data through props, use curly braces for JavaScript expressions, and nest components to compose a UI tree.
Foundations::Components & JSX.explanation: Define components as capitalized JavaScript functions that accept props and return JSX. JSX places markup-like structure beside JavaScript logic, and curly braces insert JavaScript expressions such as prop values. Compose components by rendering one component inside another, passing data through props.
Foundations::Components & JSX.returns: JSX markup representing the component's UI

example.title: A component that accepts props and returns JSX
example.explanation: A component receives a prop and returns JSX; using it as an element composes it into the application UI.

useCases.title: Reusable interface pieces
useCases.scenario: Create reusable UI elements such as buttons, cards, or navigation sections.

useCases.title: Markup with JavaScript
useCases.scenario: Keep rendering logic and displayed content together in a component file.

useCases.title: Composable UI trees
useCases.scenario: Build pages by nesting smaller components and passing each one the data it needs.

interview.question: What is a React component, and how does JSX relate to it?
interview.answer: A component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX, and JSX is a syntax extension that represents markup inside JavaScript. Components can be combined by rendering them inside other components.
interview.followUp: How do you pass data into a child? Pass attributes when rendering it; React makes those values available to the child as props.

interview.question: What rules should you follow when writing a component with JSX?
interview.answer: Use a capitalized function name and return a single JSX tree. Put JavaScript expressions inside curly braces when the rendered output needs dynamic data.
interview.followUp: How can a component render different output? Use ordinary JavaScript conditional syntax such as if, &&, or the conditional operator.

interview.question: How are components composed into a UI tree?
interview.answer: Compose a UI by nesting components in the JSX returned by another component. Supply child data through JSX attributes, which become the receiving component’s props.
interview.followUp: What should you do when sibling JSX elements need to be returned together? Wrap them in a shared parent element or an empty Fragment.

keyPoints: Treat each independently defined UI piece as a component, then combine those pieces to form the application.
The core component model is a JavaScript function whose returned result includes markup-like JSX.
JSX resembles HTML but follows stricter syntax rules, so familiar HTML may need small adjustments.
JSX is optional but is the common notation for describing the markup a component renders.

Foundations::Conditional rendering.summary: Render alternate UI by using ordinary JavaScript conditions. Choose if/else or early returns for larger branches, ternaries for either-or JSX, and && when the false case renders nothing.
Foundations::Conditional rendering.explanation: Conditional rendering uses ordinary JavaScript branching to choose which JSX a component returns or includes. Use if statements for guards and early returns, the ternary operator for either-or choices inside JSX, and && when the false branch should render nothing; a component can return null to render no UI.
Foundations::Conditional rendering.returns: A component returns JSX for the selected UI, or null when it should render nothing.

example.title: Choose and conditionally include UI
example.explanation: This component uses a ternary to choose the button label and && to show the status only when the condition is true.

useCases.title: Choose between alternate views
useCases.scenario: A component has distinct authenticated and unauthenticated layouts.

useCases.title: Include optional UI
useCases.scenario: A small indicator, action, or message should appear only when a flag is true.

useCases.title: Guard with an early return
useCases.scenario: A component should stop rendering when its required state is absent.

interview.question: How do you conditionally render JSX in React?
interview.answer: React does not add a separate conditional syntax. Write normal JavaScript branching: use if statements, the ternary operator, or &&, then return or embed the selected JSX.
interview.followUp: When is && preferable to a ternary? Use && when the false case should display nothing; use a ternary when both true and false cases need UI.

interview.question: What is the difference between a ternary and && in JSX?
interview.answer: A ternary chooses one of two JSX results: the first expression when the condition is truthy and the second when it is falsy. It works directly inside JSX braces.
interview.followUp: How would you express a one-sided condition? Replace the ternary with condition && <Element /> so the false case contributes nothing.

interview.question: When should you use an early return?
interview.answer: Use an if guard or early return when the component's larger output depends on a condition. If no output is appropriate, return null; otherwise return the alternate JSX.
interview.followUp: Why use an early return instead of deeply nested JSX? It keeps the main render path straightforward and makes the alternate state explicit.

keyPoints: Use JavaScript if statements, &&, and the ternary operator to select JSX based on conditions.
An if/else branch can return completely different JSX trees for the two states.
Use a ternary inside JSX when both condition outcomes need distinct UI.
Use && for optional JSX whose false branch should render nothing.
An if statement can choose which JSX expression the component returns before the main return path.
Return null from a component branch when that state should produce no rendered UI.
gotchas: A component cannot omit its return value; use null when its condition means that no UI should be rendered.
Returning null is the explicit way to render nothing from a component or early-return branch.

Foundations::Lists and keys.summary: Use a stable key for every item rendered from an array. The key should represent the item’s identity, not its current position, so React can match items correctly when the collection changes.
Foundations::Lists and keys.explanation: When JSX is produced from an array, give each item a stable string or number that identifies the underlying item. React uses that identity to match components across renders, so inserting, deleting, or reordering items updates the correct parts of the UI.

example.title: Render a keyed collection
example.explanation: The stable database ID identifies each person even when the collection is reordered.

useCases.title: Use a record ID
useCases.scenario: Rendering records from an API

useCases.title: Preserve identity through reordering
useCases.scenario: Displaying sortable results

useCases.title: Use key plus a separate prop
useCases.scenario: Passing identity into a child component

interview.question: Why does React require keys when rendering arrays?
interview.answer: React uses a key to associate each rendered component with the corresponding array item between renders. Stable identity lets it handle insertion, deletion, and reordering without confusing one item for another.
interview.followUp: What makes an identity suitable as a key? Use a value that belongs to the item and remains unchanged while that item remains the same; avoid values generated during rendering.

interview.question: Where must keys be unique?
interview.answer: Keys must be unique among siblings, but they do not need to be globally unique. The same key can therefore appear in separate arrays rendered in different places.
interview.followUp: What if two siblings share a key? React cannot reliably distinguish them, so choose an identifier unique within that sibling set.

interview.question: Can a component read its key through props?
interview.answer: The key is consumed by React and is not available as a component prop. If a component needs the same identifier, pass it separately, such as key={id} and userId={id}.
interview.followUp: Why separate the values? The key controls reconciliation, while the ordinary prop supplies application data to the component.

keyPoints: Every item rendered from an array needs a key whose value is a string or number.
Choose identity from the item’s data, such as a database ID, rather than from its current position.
React uses keys to connect rendered components with their underlying collection items across updates.
Place the key on the JSX element returned directly by map(), including when that element is a component.
gotchas: Do not generate keys during rendering; derive them from persistent item data.
A key only needs to be unique within its immediate sibling collection, not across the entire application.

Foundations::Props and composition.sourceTitle: Passing Props to a Component – React
Foundations::Props and composition.summary: Props are a component’s read-only inputs, passed by a parent through JSX. They let small components be configured and composed with data, callbacks, or nested JSX.
Foundations::Props and composition.explanation: A component receives one props object from its parent. The parent supplies values in JSX, while the child reads them through parameter destructuring; those values may be data, functions, or JSX, allowing components to be customized and composed without duplicating their rendering logic.

parameters.name: props
parameters.description: The single object containing values passed from the parent JSX element.

Foundations::Props and composition.returns: The component returns JSX describing its rendered UI.

example.title: Passing props to a reusable component
example.explanation: The parent configures Avatar by passing an object and a size; Avatar reads those props and renders the customized image.

useCases.title: Configure repeated UI
useCases.scenario: A parent renders many similar controls with different labels, values, or handlers.

useCases.title: Reuse presentation logic
useCases.scenario: A shared visual component needs domain data such as a person object and display dimensions.

useCases.title: Pass JSX or callbacks
useCases.scenario: A component needs custom nested content or behavior supplied by its caller.

interview.question: What are props, and how does a component read them?
interview.answer: Props are the information passed to a JSX tag. A component function receives one props object, and destructuring provides convenient access to selected values.
interview.followUp: What can a prop contain? Any JavaScript value, including objects, arrays, functions, and JSX, so callbacks and nested UI can be passed explicitly.

interview.question: How do you pass and destructure props?
interview.answer: The parent passes props in JSX, such as <Avatar person={person} size={80} />. The child declares matching names in its parameter, for example function Avatar({ person, size }).
interview.followUp: How would you provide a fallback? Use destructuring, such as size = 100; it applies only when size is missing or undefined.

interview.question: Why are props read-only?
interview.answer: Props enable parent-to-child communication and customization. They are read-only snapshots, so a child should not mutate them or treat them as local writable state.
interview.followUp: How can a child request a change? The parent can pass a function prop; the child calls it, and the parent supplies updated props on the next render.

keyPoints: Use props as the explicit communication channel between a parent and its child.
The parent owns the inputs and decides which values each child receives.
Put component inputs directly on the JSX element using named props.
Destructure the props parameter to make component inputs available as local variables.
Treat a component's props object like a function's argument bundle when defining its API.
gotchas: Do not mutate props inside a component. To change what a child displays, the parent must render it again with different props.
A destructuring default does not replace other falsy values such as 0 or null.

Foundations::Refs and the DOM.summary: Use refs to access a DOM node when React's declarative model cannot perform the needed imperative browser operation. Attach a useRef-created object to JSX and use its current value in event handlers.
Foundations::Refs and the DOM.explanation: Declare a ref with useRef(null), attach it to the JSX element through ref, and read the resulting DOM node from ref.current in an event handler. React assigns the node after it creates the element and resets the value to null when the element is removed; changing current itself does not trigger rendering.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: The initial value stored in the ref; use null when the ref will later hold a DOM node.

Foundations::Refs and the DOM.returns: A ref object with one current property. For a DOM ref, current is initially null, becomes the attached DOM node after creation, and returns to null after removal.

example.title: Focus an input with a ref
example.explanation: The ref starts as null, then React places the input DOM node in current after rendering. The click handler uses the browser focus API imperatively.

useCases.title: Focus an input
useCases.scenario: Move keyboard focus to a particular input after a user action.

useCases.title: Scroll to an element
useCases.scenario: Scroll a managed element into view in response to an interaction.

useCases.title: Measure layout
useCases.scenario: Read an element's dimensions or position for an imperative browser operation.

interview.question: How do you access a DOM element with a ref?
interview.answer: Create the ref with useRef(null), pass it to the element's ref attribute, and read ref.current from an event handler. React fills current with the DOM node after creation and sets it back to null when the node is removed.
interview.followUp: What happens if current changes? React does not re-render because ref updates are mutable storage rather than rendering data.

interview.question: When should refs be used instead of declarative React code?
interview.answer: Refs are appropriate when an imperative browser operation is required, such as focusing, scrolling, or measuring an element. They let code call browser APIs on the managed DOM node while leaving ordinary UI description declarative.
interview.followUp: Why not use state for the DOM node? State changes trigger rendering, while changing a ref does not, so a ref avoids an unnecessary render for imperative data.

interview.question: What is the lifecycle of a DOM ref?
interview.answer: An object ref from useRef is attached with JSX such as <input ref={inputRef}>. React stores the corresponding DOM node in inputRef.current, initially null, and the handler can call a method such as focus().
interview.followUp: What alternative does React support? A ref callback receives the DOM node when attached and can return cleanup for its removal.

keyPoints: Use a DOM ref for imperative tasks React does not provide declaratively, including focusing, scrolling, or measuring.
useRef returns a stable object whose current property holds the referenced value.
Initialize a DOM ref with null because no element is attached during the initial declaration.
Read current in an event handler to invoke browser APIs such as focus on the attached node.
The basic setup imports useRef, creates a ref, and passes it to the target JSX element.
Attaching ref={inputRef} makes React store that input's DOM node in the ref object.
gotchas: Use refs for imperative escape hatches, not as a replacement for declarative rendering or state.
The DOM node is available through current only after React has created the element; the initial value is null.
A callback ref can receive cleanup when its DOM node is removed; avoid assuming the node remains attached forever.

Foundations::useId.summary: Generate unique IDs for accessibility attributes with useId. React keeps them aligned between server rendering and hydration when the server and client render identical component trees.
Foundations::useId.explanation: Call useId at the top level of a component to obtain a unique string, then assign it to related accessibility attributes such as id and aria-describedby. React can produce matching IDs during server rendering and hydration when the server and client render identical component trees.
Foundations::useId.returns: A unique ID string associated with the particular useId call in the component.

example.title: Link an input to its accessible hint
example.explanation: The generated ID connects the input to its descriptive hint through accessibility attributes.

useCases.title: Connect controls with descriptions
useCases.scenario: A form control needs a descriptive hint or error message.

useCases.title: Coordinate accessible relationships
useCases.scenario: Several accessibility attributes must refer to the same generated element ID.

useCases.title: Preserve hydration-safe IDs
useCases.scenario: A component is rendered on both server and client.

interview.question: What does useId return, and what is it commonly used for?
interview.answer: useId is a Hook that returns a unique string associated with a particular useId call in a component. It is intended for IDs used by accessibility attributes, such as connecting a control with its description.
interview.followUp: Why is it useful with server rendering? It lets React generate IDs that agree between server output and client hydration, provided both sides render the same component tree.

interview.question: Where can useId be called?
interview.answer: Call useId at the top level of the component or inside a custom Hook. Do not place it in loops or conditions, because Hook calls must remain in a consistent order.
interview.followUp: How should conditional behavior be modeled instead? Extract a separate component and move the relevant state or Hook call into that component.

interview.question: What is the signature and what conditions affect hydration?
interview.answer: useId does not accept parameters. The returned value is a unique ID string associated with that specific call in that specific component.
interview.followUp: What must be true for server-generated and client-generated IDs to match? The component trees rendered on the server and client must match exactly.

keyPoints: Use useId to create unique identifiers for relationships expressed through accessibility attributes.
Invoke it at the component's top level, rather than inside nested control flow.
The Hook has no arguments; its result is determined by the component and the particular call.
Each call receives its own unique string, so separate relationships can use separate IDs.
Identical server and client trees allow the IDs to remain aligned through hydration.
gotchas: Do not call useId inside loops or conditional branches; Hooks must be called at the component or custom Hook's top level.
Server-rendered and client-rendered component trees must be identical for the generated IDs to match during hydration.

Modern React::Document metadata.summary: React 19 lets components declare document metadata with built-in <title>, <meta>, and metadata <link> elements. React automatically places these elements in the document head, even when rendered deep in the component tree.
Modern React::Document metadata.explanation: React supports rendering document metadata directly in components. When a component renders built-in <title>, <meta>, or metadata <link> elements, React hoists the corresponding DOM nodes into the document head, even when the component is nested elsewhere in the tree.

example.title: Metadata from a component
example.explanation: Rendering these built-in metadata components from a page component lets React place the title and meta elements in the document head.

useCases.title: Page-specific SEO metadata
useCases.scenario: A page component knows its own title and search metadata.

useCases.title: Data-driven document metadata
useCases.scenario: A blog or product component has data that should be reflected in the document head.

useCases.title: Client, SSR, and Server Components
useCases.scenario: The same component model must support browser rendering and server delivery.

interview.question: How does React handle metadata rendered deep in the component tree?
interview.answer: React 19 lets components render built-in <title>, <meta>, and metadata <link> elements directly. React detects them and hoists their corresponding DOM nodes into the document head, regardless of where those components occur in the tree.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from manually editing the head? It keeps metadata near the component that determines it and works across client-only apps, streaming SSR, and Server Components.

interview.question: How do you set a document title from a component?
interview.answer: Use the built-in <title> component with text as its child. React places the resulting title element in the document head, and the title text becomes the document title.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies to the child? It must be a single string, number, or object with a toString method; multiple rendered children are not valid.

interview.question: How do you add metadata from a component, and what prop constraint applies?
interview.answer: Render the built-in <meta> component with a metadata selector such as name, httpEquiv, charset, or itemProp, together with the appropriate value. React places the resulting meta element in the head.
interview.followUp: Can metadata describe an item instead of the whole document? Yes; use itemProp to annotate specific items within the document.

keyPoints: React 19 natively supports rendering document metadata tags from components.
React moves rendered <title>, <link>, and <meta> elements into the document head.
A component can render <meta> regardless of its location in the component tree.
gotchas: A <meta> element must select exactly one metadata-identifying prop from the documented alternatives.

Modern React::Stylesheets and preloading.summary: React coordinates stylesheet loading and ordering from the component tree. Use `precedence` on stylesheet links and `preload` when a resource should begin fetching before it is rendered.
Modern React::Stylesheets and preloading.explanation: React can discover resources from the component tree. Give a stylesheet a precedence value so React orders it relative to other stylesheets and waits for an external stylesheet before revealing dependent content; call preload when you know a resource will be needed and want fetching to begin early.

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: The resource URL to fetch.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options including the resource type and optional relative fetch priority.

Modern React::Stylesheets and preloading.returns: `preload` returns nothing; it provides the browser with a hint to begin downloading the resource.

example.title: Preload and render a component stylesheet
example.explanation: The component hints that its stylesheet should be fetched early, then renders the stylesheet with a precedence group so React can coordinate its order and loading.

useCases.title: Declare a local stylesheet dependency
useCases.scenario: A component needs styles before it can appear correctly.

useCases.title: Start fetching an anticipated resource
useCases.scenario: A likely navigation or upcoming render needs a stylesheet, font, image, or script soon.

useCases.title: Coordinate precedence groups
useCases.scenario: Several style systems must coexist without accidental cascade order changes.

interview.question: How does a component declare a stylesheet dependency?
interview.answer: Render a stylesheet as a `<link rel="stylesheet">` inside the component that depends on it and provide `precedence`. React uses that value to place the stylesheet relative to other stylesheets and can suspend dependent content while it loads.
interview.followUp: How can fetching begin earlier? Call `preload(href, { as: 'style' })` when rendering once you know the stylesheet will be needed; this gives the browser an early fetch hint.

interview.question: What does the `precedence` prop control?
interview.answer: React treats precedence values as ordering groups. Stylesheets with higher precedence can override stylesheets with lower precedence, while stylesheets in the same group are kept together.
interview.followUp: What determines implicit relative ranking? React considers values discovered earlier in the component tree lower and later-discovered values higher.

interview.question: What is the role of `preload`?
interview.answer: `preload` asks the browser to start fetching a resource such as a stylesheet, font, image, or external script. It is a hint rather than the stylesheet declaration itself, so the resource still needs to be used by the rendered UI.
interview.followUp: Which option controls fetch urgency? The `priority` option suggests `auto`, `high`, or `low` relative priority, with `auto` as the default.

keyPoints: Use `precedence` on stylesheet links to make React manage their document order instead of relying on incidental rendering order.
Assign higher precedence to rules intended to win over lower-ranked stylesheet groups.
A precedence group can contain external links and inline styles, allowing one ordering model across both forms.
A component may suspend while its declared external stylesheet loads, helping prevent its content from appearing without required styling.
Set preload `priority` to `auto`, `high`, or `low` to suggest relative fetch urgency.
gotchas: A stylesheet link that participates in React's ordering behavior must include `precedence`; omitting it prevents that coordination.
Precedence is relative to discovery order, so introducing values in a different component-tree order can change which rules win.

Performance::React Compiler.summary: React Compiler is a build-time optimizer that automatically memoizes React components, values, and calculations. It follows the Rules of React so most code can gain update-performance improvements without manual memoization.
Performance::React Compiler.explanation: React Compiler analyzes React components and Hooks during the build, then automatically memoizes components, values, and calculations when appropriate. It relies on the Rules of React; code that may violate them can be skipped safely, while useMemo and useCallback remain available when precise manual control is needed.

example.title: Compiler-friendly component
example.explanation: With the React Compiler enabled in the build, the component and its render-time calculation can be memoized automatically without adding manual memoization hooks.

useCases.title: Skip cascading re-renders
useCases.scenario: A parent update causes unaffected descendants to render again.

useCases.title: Reuse expensive calculations
useCases.scenario: A component repeatedly performs costly pure work during rendering.

useCases.title: Prefer compiler inference
useCases.scenario: A new codebase wants fewer hand-written memoization decisions.

interview.question: What does React Compiler do?
interview.answer: React Compiler is a build-time tool that analyzes React code and inserts automatic memoization. It can reduce cascading child re-renders and repeated expensive calculations without requiring manual useMemo, useCallback, or memo in typical new code.
interview.followUp: What happens when code violates the Rules of React? The compiler can safely skip optimization for the affected component or Hook instead of changing its behavior.

interview.question: Which performance problems does it target?
interview.answer: It primarily improves update performance. The compiler can avoid re-rendering unchanged parts of a component tree and reuse expensive render-time calculations when its analysis determines that reuse is valid.
interview.followUp: Does it eliminate every render? No. Its optimization targets unnecessary work; it does not make memoization a semantic guarantee.

interview.question: Are useMemo and useCallback still needed?
interview.answer: The compiler infers memoization from its analysis and heuristics by default. useMemo and useCallback still work as escape hatches when a developer needs more precise control over what is memoized.
interview.followUp: Should existing manual memoization always be removed? Not automatically; remove it when appropriate, but retain explicit memoization when deliberate control or compatibility requires it.

keyPoints: Optimization happens during the build rather than through a runtime-only feature.
The compiler is designed for ordinary JavaScript and uses React’s rules as part of its analysis.
Its generated optimization can provide the effect of manually memoizing components and values.
A central benefit is reducing propagation of updates into unaffected portions of the UI.
Render-time calculations that are costly may be cached automatically when the compiler determines that it is safe.
Default behavior is inferred rather than requiring annotations on every component.
gotchas: The compiler does not force optimization onto code that appears to violate the Rules of React; it can leave affected components or Hooks unoptimized.

Performance::useDeferredValue.summary: Defer updating a non-critical part of the UI so urgent interactions, such as typing, stay responsive while React prepares the expensive view.
Performance::useDeferredValue.explanation: Call the Hook with a value whose update should not block urgent UI. React returns the previous value first during an update, then attempts a background render with the new value, allowing an expensive child view to lag briefly while input-driven UI stays responsive.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to defer; it can have any type.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: Optional value used during the component’s initial render. If omitted, the initial render is not deferred.

Performance::useDeferredValue.returns: Returns the current deferred value. On the initial render it is initialValue, if supplied, otherwise value; during updates React may first return the previous value and later render with the new value.

example.title: Keep search input responsive
example.explanation: The input uses the immediate query, while the results receive a deferred query and can continue showing older content during an update.

useCases.title: Responsive search
useCases.scenario: A controlled search field updates immediately while a costly result list consumes deferredQuery.

useCases.title: Expensive derived view
useCases.scenario: A large visualization or filtered collection can render behind the latest controls.

useCases.title: Stale content during loading
useCases.scenario: A deferred query can keep previous results visible while new Suspense-driven content loads.

interview.question: What problem does useDeferredValue solve?
interview.answer: It returns a deferred version of the supplied value. During an update, React can first render with the old value and then try a background render with the new one, so urgent UI can update before an expensive view.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from debouncing? It has no fixed delay; React schedules an interruptible background render rather than waiting for a timer.

interview.question: What does the optional initialValue parameter do?
interview.answer: The Hook takes the value to defer and optionally an initialValue. The initial value is used only for the component’s initial render; later updates use the previous value first when React defers the work.
interview.followUp: What happens if initialValue is omitted? The first render uses the supplied value because React has no earlier version to display.

interview.question: How would you use this Hook for a searchable view?
interview.answer: The input should read the immediate state, while an expensive child receives the deferred value. This lets the input reflect typing immediately while the child may temporarily render stale content.
interview.followUp: What should be passed to the Hook? Prefer primitives or objects created outside rendering, because a newly created object changes identity on every render.

keyPoints: Use it when a non-critical UI section is expensive to update and should yield to more urgent interaction.
Invoke the Hook at component scope, not conditionally or inside nested functions.
The deferred value can lag behind the latest value, allowing the current UI to remain responsive.
React separately attempts to render the updated value in the background.
gotchas: Prefer primitive values, or objects created outside rendering; creating a new object during every render can trigger unnecessary background renders.
Inside a Transition, the update is already deferred, so this Hook does not create another deferred render.
Without initialValue, the first render uses the supplied value because no previous value exists.

Performance::useMemo and useCallback.summary: useMemo caches a calculation result; useCallback caches a function definition. Use either when stable identity enables a real optimization, such as skipping an optimized child render or avoiding unnecessary Effect work.
Performance::useMemo and useCallback.explanation: useMemo caches the result of a calculation, whereas useCallback caches the function itself. Both are performance optimizations for stabilizing values passed to optimized children or used as dependencies; use them when identity affects a real optimization, not by default.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Function or calculation to cache. useMemo calls the calculation; useCallback retains the function without calling it.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Inline array of all reactive values used by fn; React compares entries with Object.is.

Performance::useMemo and useCallback.returns: useMemo returns the cached calculation result. useCallback returns the cached function definition.

example.title: Stable props for an optimized child
example.explanation: useMemo preserves the derived object identity, while useCallback preserves the handler identity; memo can then skip Button renders when its props remain unchanged.

useCases.title: Skip unnecessary child renders
useCases.scenario: A memoized child receives a callback prop; useCallback keeps that prop identity stable when its inputs are unchanged.

useCases.title: Stabilize derived values
useCases.scenario: A calculation creates an object, array, or derived data passed to an optimized child; useMemo preserves its identity until relevant inputs change.

useCases.title: Control Effect dependencies
useCases.scenario: An Effect depends on a callback or derived value whose identity would otherwise change on every render; memoize it when that prevents avoidable Effect work.

interview.question: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
interview.answer: useMemo caches the value returned by calling a calculation function. useCallback caches the function definition itself and does not invoke it.
interview.followUp: How are they conceptually related? useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps).

interview.question: How should dependencies be selected?
interview.answer: Pass every value from the component that the calculation or callback reads in its dependency list. React compares dependencies with Object.is and recalculates or returns a new function when one changes.
interview.followUp: What happens with an omitted dependency? The hook cannot correctly track reactive inputs, so the cached result or callback can become stale; restructure the code or specify the complete list.

interview.question: When should these hooks be used?
interview.answer: They are useful when a stable identity enables a concrete optimization, such as allowing memo to skip a child render, or when a stable value or callback prevents an Effect from running unnecessarily. They add complexity and should not be used indiscriminately.
interview.followUp: What alternative can reduce the need for them? React Compiler can automatically memoize in supported code, while the hooks remain available when precise manual control is needed.

keyPoints: useCallback returns the same function identity across renders while its dependencies are unchanged.
Provide the function to retain and a dependency list containing each reactive value used by that function.
Together, the hooks can stabilize object-like values and callbacks passed as props to an optimized child.
useCallback stores the callback rather than its return value; useMemo stores the calculation’s return value.
Place the hook at component top level around a callback whose identity matters to a child optimization or dependency list.
gotchas: Call the Hooks only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; do not place them in loops or conditions.

Performance::useTransition.summary: useTransition marks non-urgent state updates as Transitions so React can render them in the background while urgent interactions stay responsive. It also provides isPending for showing transition progress.
Performance::useTransition.explanation: At component level, call useTransition to obtain a pending indicator and a function for scheduling non-urgent state updates. Pass a synchronous callback to startTransition; React marks updates performed during that callback as transitions so urgent work can interrupt them. In React 19, transition callbacks may also be async, but updates after an await need another transition wrapper.
Performance::useTransition.returns: An array containing exactly two items: isPending, a boolean indicating whether a Transition is pending, and startTransition, a function that marks updates as a Transition.

example.title: Marking a tab change as a transition
example.explanation: Wraps the tab state update in a transition and uses isPending to expose progress.

useCases.title: Keep tab navigation responsive
useCases.scenario: A tab switch changes a large panel and may require substantial rendering.

useCases.title: Prioritize text input over results
useCases.scenario: A search control should accept typing while result rendering catches up.

useCases.title: Show pending navigation feedback
useCases.scenario: A route or view change needs visible progress without blocking interaction.

interview.question: What does useTransition return?
interview.answer: useTransition returns exactly two values: isPending and startTransition. The boolean indicates whether a transition is pending, while the function marks state updates performed by its callback as transitions.
interview.followUp: How can code outside a component start a transition? Use the standalone startTransition API, which can mark updates but does not provide the Hook's isPending indicator.

interview.question: How do you mark an update as a transition?
interview.answer: Call the Hook at the top level of a component or custom Hook, then call startTransition with a callback around the non-urgent state update. React can let urgent updates interrupt that transition work.
interview.followUp: What happens if an update occurs after an async request? Wrap that later update in another startTransition call so it is marked as transition work.

interview.question: When should useTransition be used instead of standalone startTransition?
interview.answer: The callback supplied to startTransition is invoked immediately, and state updates made while it runs are marked as transitions. The Hook also exposes isPending so the UI can show progress while the transition is active.
interview.followUp: Why might a component prefer the standalone API? A non-component context such as a data library may need to start the transition, but only the Hook supplies a pending flag.

keyPoints: It lets React render part of the interface in the background instead of treating every update as equally urgent.
Call it at the component’s top level, not conditionally or inside event-specific branches.
Use isPending to display progress feedback or adjust controls while transition work remains pending.
Use startTransition to identify state updates whose rendering can be deferred in favor of urgent interaction.
All state updates performed during the callback are classified as transition updates.
The Hook has no configuration arguments; its behavior is controlled through the returned function.
gotchas: The callback passed to startTransition must be synchronous; do not make it an async function when relying on the documented synchronous callback behavior.
After an asynchronous request, wrap subsequent state updates in another startTransition call so React continues treating them as transition work.
Call useTransition only within a component or custom Hook, following the Rules of Hooks.
Code outside components cannot use this Hook; use the standalone startTransition API when no component or custom Hook is available.

Server & client::Context as a provider.summary: React 19 lets you render a context object directly as a provider, making shared values available to descendants without passing props through every layer.
Server & client::Context as a provider.explanation: Create a context, then render that context as a provider with a value. Every descendant can read the nearest provider's value with useContext or use; the provider must be above the component that reads it, and nested providers can override outer values.

parameters.name: SomeContext
parameters.description: The context object created by createContext; render it as the provider element.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value made available to descendants that read this context.

Server & client::Context as a provider.returns: A provider element that makes value available to matching descendant consumers.

example.title: Providing context with the context element
example.explanation: The provider supplies a theme to every descendant, and Button reads the nearest value without receiving a theme prop.

useCases.title: Share theme or locale configuration
useCases.scenario: Application-wide preferences

useCases.title: Expose current user data to nested client components
useCases.scenario: Authenticated interfaces

useCases.title: Provide changing state and its update functions to a subtree
useCases.scenario: Stateful coordination

interview.question: How do you provide context in React 19?
interview.answer: Starting in React 19, the context object itself can be rendered as the provider, using a value prop. Descendants can read the nearest value with useContext or use; older React versions use SomeContext.Provider.
interview.followUp: What happens with nested providers? The consumer receives the value from the closest corresponding provider above it, so an inner provider overrides an outer one.

interview.question: How does React choose a context value?
interview.answer: Call useContext with the context created by createContext. React searches upward from the calling component and returns the value supplied by the closest matching provider, or the context's default when none exists.
interview.followUp: Can a consumer read a provider rendered in the same component? No; the provider must be above the component performing the read.

interview.question: How can context provide changing shared state?
interview.answer: A context provider's value can have any type and is passed to all descendants reading that context, regardless of their depth. To change it over time, keep the value in parent state and pass that state to the provider.
interview.followUp: How can a Server Component render context? It cannot create context, but it can render a context imported from a 'use client' module; Client Components below can read it.

keyPoints: React 19 lets the context object serve directly as the provider element.
The value prop reaches matching consumers at any descendant depth.
Consumers use the innermost matching provider when providers are nested.
A provider can supply primitives, objects, functions, or other values.

Server & client::Server Components.summary: Server Components render ahead of bundling in a separate server environment, either at build time or per request. They keep data access and heavy rendering on the server while interactive behavior stays in intentional Client Component boundaries.
Server & client::Server Components.explanation: A Server Component executes in a separate server environment before the application is bundled. It may run at build time or per request, read files or access a data layer directly, and pass serializable data or JSX into Client Components. Because it is not sent to the browser, interactive behavior belongs in a client subtree marked with "use client".
Server & client::Server Components.syntax: async function Component(props) { /* server-side rendering and data access */ }
Server & client::Server Components.returns: Rendered data and JSX that can be passed to Client Components; the page may be rendered at build time or per request.

example.title: Server-render data and delegate interaction
example.explanation: The server component reads data directly, while the client component provides interaction.

useCases.title: Build-time content generation
useCases.scenario: A mostly static page needs filesystem content or fetched static data.

useCases.title: Request-time data rendering
useCases.scenario: A page needs direct access to a database or other server-side data layer.

useCases.title: Server-rendered UI with client islands
useCases.scenario: A data-heavy view needs only small interactive controls in the browser.

interview.question: What is a Server Component?
interview.answer: A Server Component renders ahead of bundling in an environment separate from the client app or SSR server. It can run during a build or for each request, and its output is not included as client JavaScript.
interview.followUp: How would you add a button to it? Put the button in a Client Component and pass it serializable props or JSX from the Server Component.

interview.question: Why use Server Components for data-heavy UI?
interview.answer: Use a Server Component for data access when the data can be fetched on the server or at build time. It can read the filesystem or access the data layer directly, avoiding the need to construct an API for that access.
interview.followUp: Can it update when data changes? Yes: run or re-fetch the Server Component from the server so it accesses current data and renders again.

interview.question: How do Server and Client Components work together?
interview.answer: The boundary is created by the client-marking directive: code in that module and its transitive dependencies is client code. Components outside that client subtree are Server Components by default in an RSC application.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies to props crossing the boundary? They must be serializable, because the server sends them to the client.

keyPoints: They support static generation at build time and request-time rendering on a web server.
Static content can be produced without deploying a web server for the component execution.
Rendering happens before bundling, and Server Components can provide data or JSX to interactive descendants.

Server & client::Server Functions.summary: Server Functions let Client Components call async server-side functions through React-managed requests. Mark functions with 'use server'; use them primarily for authorized mutations and invoke them in Actions or Transitions.
Server & client::Server Functions.explanation: A Server Function is an async function marked with 'use server' so client code can invoke work on the server. React and the framework arrange a network request, serialize arguments and any returned value, and expose the function through a reference; use it for authorized mutations rather than ordinary data fetching.

parameters.name: ...args
parameters.description: Arguments passed by client code; React serializes a copy for the server request. The page does not prescribe a fixed parameter list.

Server & client::Server Functions.returns: A promise resolving to the Server Function's serialized return value; if no value is returned, it resolves without a useful result.

example.title: Calling a Server Function from a client component
example.explanation: A module-level directive exposes the exported async function to client code. React turns the imported reference into a server request; the client invokes it inside a Transition and can await its promise.

useCases.title: Form mutations
useCases.scenario: A form submission needs to create, update, or delete server-side data.

useCases.title: Interactive mutations
useCases.scenario: A client interaction must trigger a server-side state change without a hand-written API endpoint.

useCases.title: Passing server operations as props
useCases.scenario: A Server Component has a server operation that a Client Component needs to invoke.

interview.question: What is a Server Function?
interview.answer: A Server Function is an async server-side function marked with 'use server'. When client code calls its reference, React sends a request to execute it and returns a promise for the serialized result.
interview.followUp: What must be protected? Treat arguments as untrusted input and authorize mutations on the server, because exposed functions can be called from client code.

interview.question: How do you define and import one?
interview.answer: Put 'use server' at the top of an async function, or at module scope to mark all exported functions. A module directive enables importing those exports from client code; a function directive marks one function.
interview.followUp: Why must it be async? The underlying network call is asynchronous, so Server Functions require async functions.

interview.question: How should a client invoke a Server Function?
interview.answer: Server Functions are intended for mutations that update server-side state. Call them in a Transition, or pass one to a form action or formAction, which invokes it through the form's action flow.
interview.followUp: How can the client consume a result? Await the promise returned by the Server Function.

keyPoints: They let Client Components invoke asynchronous server work without implementing a separate client-side API call.
The call crosses the network: React requests server execution and returns the function's result to the caller.
A Server Component may pass a function as a prop, while client code may import module-level Server Functions.

State & effects::Effects and synchroniza.summary: Use Effects to synchronize React with external systems when rendering alone cannot express the work. They run after commits and should re-run only when their reactive dependencies require synchronization.
State & effects::Effects and synchroniza.explanation: An Effect is React’s mechanism for running synchronization code after a commit, when rendering alone cannot express an interaction with an external system. Declare it with useEffect, list every reactive value it reads as a dependency, and return cleanup when synchronization must be stopped or reversed.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: A callback containing synchronization code; it may return cleanup code.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional reactive values read by the callback.

State & effects::Effects and synchroniza.returns: The page does not specify a standalone return value for useEffect; its setup callback may return a cleanup function.

example.title: Synchronize a video element
example.explanation: The Effect synchronizes the browser video element with the React state after rendering. The dependency makes it run again only when playback state changes.

useCases.title: Synchronize an external widget
useCases.scenario: A component controls a browser or third-party widget whose imperative API must reflect React state.

useCases.title: Manage an external connection
useCases.scenario: A component connects to a service whose configuration changes with props or state.

useCases.title: React to rendering-driven synchronization
useCases.scenario: A component performs work caused by being displayed or by changed reactive inputs rather than a specific user event.

related: You Might Not Need an Effect

interview.question: When should you use an Effect?
interview.answer: Use an Effect when a component must synchronize with something outside React, such as a browser API, network, or third-party library. Rendering should remain focused on describing the UI.
interview.followUp: What should happen when synchronization is no longer needed? Return cleanup from the Effect so React can stop or undo the external synchronization.

interview.question: How do dependencies control an Effect?
interview.answer: Call useEffect at the component’s top level and place the synchronization code in its callback. The dependency list states which reactive values determine when React must repeat the synchronization.
interview.followUp: How does React decide whether to repeat it? It skips the Effect only when every listed dependency has the same value as in the previous render.

interview.question: When does an Effect run?
interview.answer: Effects run after the commit, once the screen has been updated. This timing makes them suitable for coordinating React with external systems rather than producing JSX.
interview.followUp: Why not perform the synchronization during rendering? Rendering must stay free of this kind of external work so React can render predictably and potentially restart rendering.

keyPoints: Use Effects to coordinate a component with external APIs, network services, browser features, or other non-React systems.
The synchronization callback runs after React commits the rendered result to the screen.
Import useEffect and call it at the top level of the component.
Without a dependency strategy, React reruns the Effect after each commit.
Provide dependencies so synchronization repeats only when relevant reactive inputs change.
React uses the dependency values from the previous render to decide whether to skip the next run.
gotchas: Effects happen after the screen is updated, so they should not be used to calculate the rendered output itself.
React compares dependencies from the previous render; omitting a reactive value can leave the external system out of sync.
An Effect without deliberate dependencies runs after every commit, which can cause unnecessary synchronization.

State & effects::Reducers & context.sourceTitle: Scaling Up With Reducer and Context
State & effects::Reducers & context.summary: Combine useReducer with context to centralize complex state transitions and make state plus dispatch available throughout a component subtree without prop drilling.
State & effects::Reducers & context.explanation: A reducer centralizes transitions from state and actions, while separate contexts expose the resulting state and dispatch function to descendants without prop drilling. A provider component owns useReducer; consumers read whichever context they need and dispatch actions to request updates.

parameters.name: reducer
parameters.description: Pure function receiving current state and an action, then returning the next state.

parameters.name: initialArg
parameters.description: Initial state value, or input passed to init when initialization is customized.

parameters.name: init
parameters.description: Optional initializer that derives the initial state from initialArg.

State & effects::Reducers & context.returns: useReducer returns the current state and a dispatch function.

example.title: Reducer state shared through context
example.explanation: A provider owns the reducer, exposes state and dispatch through separate contexts, and a descendant dispatches an action without receiving props.

useCases.title: Centralize transitions
useCases.scenario: A complex screen has many related updates spread across event handlers.

useCases.title: Avoid prop drilling
useCases.scenario: Deep descendants need to read shared state.

useCases.title: Share state and dispatch
useCases.scenario: Nested components both display and modify one state model.

interview.question: When is useReducer useful?
interview.answer: useReducer centralizes state-transition logic in a reducer that receives the current state and an action and returns the next state. Event handlers dispatch actions instead of implementing every transition themselves.
interview.followUp: Why must the reducer be pure? Because reducers run during rendering, so identical inputs must produce identical outputs and side effects must be avoided.

interview.question: How do you combine a reducer with context?
interview.answer: Use two contexts: one for the current state and one for the dispatch function. The provider calls useReducer and supplies both values, allowing descendants to read state or dispatch actions without prop drilling.
interview.followUp: Why separate the contexts? A component that only dispatches can subscribe to the dispatch context without also consuming the state value.

interview.question: What does useReducer return?
interview.answer: useReducer(reducer, initialArg, init?) returns the current state and a dispatch function. Dispatching an action causes React to run the reducer and use its returned value as the next state.
interview.followUp: Where may useReducer be called? Only at the top level of a component or custom Hook, not inside loops or conditions.

keyPoints: Move related transition rules into one reducer when many event handlers make state updates difficult to follow.
Use context to make reducer state available to descendants without manually forwarding it through every layer.
A provider component can own the reducer while deeply nested components read and update the shared screen state.
The component calling useReducer should place both context providers around the relevant subtree.
Consumers choose the state context for reading or the dispatch context for sending actions.
gotchas: Context avoids explicitly threading the values through every intermediate component, but consumers still need the appropriate provider above them.
